why: Reading chapters in some order scores the sum of prefix sums, so the chapter read k-th is counted (n-k+1) times. Swapping two adjacent chapters shows the larger one should come first: sort descending and weight by n, n-1, ..., 1.
hints: Write the total as a sum of prefix sums. How many times is the first chapter you read counted? The last?
The chapter in position k (1-based) contributes (n - k + 1) * value. An exchange argument says the biggest value should get the biggest multiplier.
Sort memory descending and return sum of (n - i) * memory[i] for 0-based i. O(n log n).
pitfalls: Values can be negative; descending order still holds, and negatives land where they are counted fewest times.
The total can exceed 32-bit; use 64-bit in other languages.
statement:
A course has n chapters; reading chapter i is worth memory[i] points (it may be negative). You read every chapter exactly once, in an order you choose. When you read a chapter you also revisit all chapters read before it, so you score the sum of all chapters read so far, including the current one.

Return the maximum possible total score.

Worked example: memory = [3, 4, 5]. Read in order 5, 4, 3:

  • Read 5: score 5.
  • Read 4: score 5 + 4 = 9.
  • Read 3: score 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
  • Total 5 + 9 + 12 = 26. Any other order is lower; for example 3, 4, 5 gives 3 + 7 + 12 = 22.
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5
  • -10^9 ≤ memory[i] ≤ 10^9
